lessons.title: Simple harmonic motion
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — oscillations and waves (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define SHM (a = −ω²x) and use x = A cos ωt, v = ±ω√(A² − x²), v_max = ωA and a_max = ω²A
Use T = 2π√(m/k) for a mass on a spring and T = 2π√(l/g) for a simple pendulum
Describe the energy changes in SHM, damping and resonance
reviewNotes: Derivation of T = 2π√(m/k) from a = −ω²x is shown only in outline.
Damping types are described qualitatively; check how much the syllabus expects.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Definition of SHM
blocks.md:
A body performs **simple harmonic motion** when its acceleration is proportional to its displacement from the equilibrium position and always directed towards it: **a = −ω²x**.

Solution: x = A cos ωt (if released from x = A at t = 0), with amplitude A, angular frequency ω = 2π/T = 2πf. Then v = −ωA sin ωt and **v = ±ω√(A² − x²)**.

blocks.title: Maxima and periods
blocks.md:
- Maximum speed (at equilibrium): v_max = ωA
- Maximum acceleration (at the extremes): a_max = ω²A
- Mass on a spring: ω² = k/m, so **T = 2π√(m/k)**
- Simple pendulum (small angles, below about 10°): **T = 2π√(l/g)**

The period does not depend on the amplitude (for these two cases) or on the mass of the pendulum bob.

blocks.caption: Displacement–time graph of SHM starting at the maximum: x = A cos ωt.
blocks.alt: A cosine curve over two periods with its maximum amplitude A and the period T marked.

blocks.title: Energy, damping and resonance
blocks.md:
Total energy E = ½mω²A² = ½kA² is constant (no damping); it changes between kinetic E_k = ½mω²(A² − x²) and potential ½mω²x². Kinetic energy is maximum at the centre; potential energy at the ends.

**Damping** (friction, air) removes energy and the amplitude decays: light, critical (fastest return without oscillation) and heavy. **Resonance**: when a driving frequency equals the natural frequency the amplitude becomes large.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using the pendulum formula for a large amplitude.
- Thinking acceleration is greatest at the centre: it is zero there (the speed is greatest).
- Setting the calculator in degrees for cos ωt: ωt is in **radians**.
- Forgetting that a = −ω²x has a minus sign: the acceleration is opposite to the displacement.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Mass on a spring
blocks.statement: A 0.50 kg mass on a spring of k = 200 N/m oscillates with amplitude 5.0 cm. Find ω, T, the maximum speed and the maximum acceleration.
blocks.answer: ω = 20 rad/s, T = 0.31 s, v_max = 1.0 m/s, a_max = 20 m/s²

blocks.title: Example 2 — Speed and energy at a point
blocks.statement: For the same oscillator, find the speed and the kinetic energy when the displacement is 3.0 cm.
steps: E_k = ½mv² = ½ × 0.50 × 0.80² = 0.16 J. Total energy ½kA² = 0.25 J, so E_p = 0.09 J.

lessons.title: Progressive waves, superposition and interference
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — oscillations and waves (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use v = fλ and relate phase difference to path difference; distinguish transverse and longitudinal waves
State the principle of superposition and the conditions for constructive and destructive interference
Use Young's double-slit formula λ = ax/D and describe diffraction at a gap
reviewNotes: Diffraction grating and single-slit minimum formula are placed in the Upper Sixth pack; check whether the syllabus puts them here.
The approximation D ≫ a is assumed.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Waves
blocks.md:
A **progressive wave** transfers energy without transferring matter. **Transverse**: vibration ⟂ direction of travel (light, water ripples, waves on a string). **Longitudinal**: vibration ∥ direction of travel (sound; compressions and rarefactions). Only transverse waves can be **polarised**.

**v = fλ**. A path difference Δx gives a phase difference **Δφ = 2πΔx/λ**. The intensity of a wave is proportional to the (amplitude)².

blocks.title: Superposition and interference
blocks.md:
**Principle of superposition**: when two or more waves meet, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements.

For two **coherent** sources (constant phase difference, same frequency): constructive interference when the path difference is **nλ** (n = 0, 1, 2…); destructive when it is **(n + ½)λ**.

blocks.caption: Young's double-slit arrangement (not to scale): bright fringes of separation w on the screen.
blocks.alt: A source, a barrier with two slits a distance a apart, a screen at distance D and bright fringes marked on the screen.

blocks.title: Young's double slit and diffraction
blocks.md:
Two narrow slits a apart, screen at distance D (D ≫ a): fringe separation **w = λD/a** (fringes are equally spaced). Laser light and slit separations of a fraction of a millimetre give visible fringes.

**Diffraction**: waves spread when passing through a gap or round an obstacle; the effect is greatest when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength. Single-slit diffraction gives a wide central maximum.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting to convert nm to m (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m) or mm to m.
- Using the slit-to-screen distance in cm with a in mm without converting.
- Thinking two torch beams interfere: they are not coherent.
- Saying light waves are longitudinal: light is transverse (polarisation proves it).

blocks.title: Example 1 — Fringe separation
blocks.statement: Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.50 mm apart onto a screen 2.0 m away. Find the fringe separation.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Two loudspeakers
blocks.statement: Two in-phase loudspeakers emit a note of frequency 170 Hz (speed of sound 340 m/s). A listener is 4.0 m from one and 5.0 m from the other. What does she hear?
steps: Path difference = 5.0 − 4.0 = 1.0 m = λ/2 (half a wavelength).
The waves arrive in antiphase: destructive interference, so a quiet spot (minimum).

lessons.title: Standing waves on strings and in pipes
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — oscillations and waves (to be checked against the official syllabus)

objectives: Explain how a standing wave forms and describe nodes, antinodes and the harmonics
Use f = nv/2L for a string, and the pipe formulae for open and closed pipes
Use v = √(T/μ) for the speed of waves on a stretched string
reviewNotes: End correction is mentioned without a formula; check the syllabus for its use.
The speed of sound in air is taken as 340 m/s.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Formation of standing waves
blocks.md:
A **standing (stationary) wave** forms when two progressive waves of the same frequency and amplitude travelling in opposite directions superpose (typically a wave and its reflection). It has **nodes** (zero amplitude) and **antinodes** (maximum amplitude), a distance λ/2 apart. Energy is not transferred along the wave.

Between two adjacent nodes all points vibrate in phase; points on either side of a node vibrate in antiphase.

blocks.title: Strings and pipes
blocks.md:
**String fixed at both ends**: a node at each end, so L = nλ/2 and **f_n = nv/2L** (n = 1, 2, 3…). Wave speed on the string: **v = √(T/μ)** (T = tension, μ = mass per unit length).

**Pipe open at both ends** (antinode at each end): f_n = nv/2L (all harmonics). **Pipe closed at one end** (node at closed end, antinode at the open end): **f = (2n − 1)v/4L**: odd harmonics only; the fundamental is v/4L.

blocks.caption: The first three harmonics of a string fixed at both ends (the envelope of the vibration).
blocks.alt: Three stacked drawings of a string fixed at both ends showing one, two and three half wavelengths.

blocks.title: Practical notes
blocks.md: In a real pipe the antinode forms slightly outside the open end (**end correction**), so the effective length is a little longer than the pipe. A stretched string produces higher notes with higher tension, shorter length or smaller mass per unit length. Resonance tubes can be used to measure the speed of sound.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Treating the closed end of a pipe as an antinode (it is a node).
- Using f = nv/2L for a closed pipe.
- Confusing the distance between adjacent nodes (λ/2) with the wavelength.
- Using μ in g/m: convert to kg/m.

blocks.title: Example 1 — A guitar string
blocks.statement: A string 0.65 m long has mass per unit length 1.0 × 10⁻³ kg/m and tension 40 N. Find the wave speed and the fundamental frequency.
steps: f₁ = v/2L = 200 ÷ (2 × 0.65) = 154 Hz; the next harmonics are 308 Hz and 462 Hz.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Pipes
blocks.statement: A pipe 0.34 m long (speed of sound 340 m/s) is open at both ends, then closed at one end. Find the fundamental frequency in each case.
steps: Closed pipe: f₁ = v/4L = 340 ÷ 1.36 = 250 Hz. The next resonance is 3f₁ = 750 Hz.
